title: Platform-eng runtime choice rapid brief
summary: Concise seller-facing brief to help platform engineering buyers decide between managing a self-hosted inference stack (vLLM/TGI/TensorRT-LLM) vs adopting Redwood (hosted, dedicated, private). Prioritizes operational risk, predictable unit economics, and migration/rollback playbooks.
audience: Platform engineering leads, solutions engineers, sales engineering, GTM reps
key_messages: Self-hosted stacks can deliver peak-path cost savings but shift unpredictability to operator time and hidden infra debt.
Redwood offers a single runtime and operational surface that makes rollouts, canarying, and fallback policies consistent whether hosted, dedicated, or private.
For teams that require strict data isolation but not full ops ownership, Redwood Private provides the compliance controls with operator-friendly automation.
We win when buyers are evaluating medium-to-high throughput production workloads where latency SLOs and cost-per-token variability matter more than marginal raw inference cost.
Position Redwood as the insurance policy: lower TCO volatility, faster time-to-value, and easier model swap/rollback than a bespoke vLLM/TGI deployment.

Highlight practical migration lanes: start with hosted for experimentation, shift to dedicated as throughput stabilizes, and move to private only when compliance or latency in-region requirements force it.
competitive_deltas: Operator effort: vLLM/TGI/TensorRT stacks require continuous tuning (batching thresholds, kernel choices, KV cache sizing). Redwood centralizes these decisions and surfaces recommendations.
SLO guarantees: self-hosted lacks uniform SLAs across regions and teams; Redwood Dedicated includes predictable throughput contracts and documented fallbacks.
Model lifecycle: self-hosted flows often tie model version to infra configs; Redwood decouples model versioning from hardware with safe rollout primitives.

Failure modes: GPU OOM, degraded quantized quality, or kernel regressions are common in self-hosted stacks. Redwood’s verification + telemetry pipeline detects regressions and can auto-fallback to compatible variants.
Unit economics stability: raw token cost may look lower on well-tuned self-hosting but hidden costs (engineering hours, incident toil, cold-start inefficiencies) typically erode that advantage.

Edge cases: TensorRT-LLM can beat others on latency for a narrow set of models/hardware — we acknowledge that and position Redwood’s private/dedicated options for those buyers rather than deny the technical parity.
tactical_hooks: Ask: 'What is your SLO for p99 latency and how does it affect monthly ops headcount?' Use this to surface ops tax.
Offer a short pilot: 2-week hosted proof-of-performance with observability export and a cost-sensitivity report comparing identical workload on self-hosted assumptions.
Migration hook: Provide a one-page checklist for moving from vLLM/TGI pilot to Redwood Dedicated without code rewrites (config mapping + KV cache sizing guide).
Risk-reversal: SLA-backed dedicated capacity and a documented rollback path to prior model versions to mitigate upgrade fears.
Play the quantization safe path: show how Redwood can run quantized variants with A/B gating and quality monitoring so buyers don't fear accuracy regressions when optimizing cost.
objections_and_rebuttals: Objection: 'We can run it cheaper on our infra.' Rebuttal: 'Show us 6 months of infra + ops hours costs; we’ll model end-to-end TCO and likely find hidden ops and variability that blur the margin.'
Objection: 'We need full control (kernel selection, custom ops).' Rebuttal: 'Redwood Private/Dedicated exposes kernel-selection knobs and supports custom hooks; control without full ops ownership.'
Objection: 'Open-source gives us vendor independence.' Rebuttal: 'You still carry the build-and-maintain burden — vendor independence vs. predictable SLAs and engineering leverage tradeoff.'

Objection: 'Latency-sensitive workloads need TensorRT on-prem.' Rebuttal: 'Agree for edge low-latency hot paths — propose hybrid: keep the hot path private with Redwood + use Redwood routing to fallback elsewhere for capacity spikes.'
win_conditions: Buyer has production throughput > 5M tokens/day or expects rapid growth in 3 months.
Buyer lacks >1 FTE dedicated to LLM infra tuning or is unwilling to absorb SRE cost for model regressions.
Regulatory/compliance needs that preclude fully hosted public cloud but allow private deployments (VPC/HSM) — positions Redwood Private.
Buyer values predictable unit economics and prefers a single contract for infra + operational SLAs rather than building internal platform features.
action_items: Create a 2-week hosted pilot template (billing + metrics export + customer checklist).
Build a side-by-side TCO spreadsheet for common infra shapes (1xA100, 4xA10, 8xH100 node examples) and share with AE pack.
Update demo scripts to include a rollback/canary flow and cost-sensitivity dashboard export.
Produce a short tech note for SEs explaining where TensorRT-LLM materially outperforms and recommended customer segmentation for private offering.
rough_notes:
- quick mental model: self-hosted = variable unit price + fixed ops tax; managed = stable unit price + lower ops tax.
- buyers we lose to vLLM often cite 'control' or 'cost' — two different personas.
- persona1: infra-first platform team; cares about kernel choice and license costs. persona2: product team; cares about time-to-feature and predictable invoices.
- short A/B experiment: run same prompt set on (1) tuned vLLM at peak throughput (2) Redwood Dedicated config, capture p50/p95/p99 and cost-per-1M-tokens.
- checklist for technical buyers: data residency, KMS, monitoring hooks, rollout cadence, incident playbook.
- unresolved: should we publish a public 'cost model FAQ' vs a gated TCO tool? recommend gated for early leads.
- slack refs: #gtm-inference, #se-ops; add DE to pilot onboarding thread.
